physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-an.prompt: The PT asked the aide to guard a seated knee bend that stays in the sagittal plane (forward and back). The patient starts kicking the leg out to the side. What should the aide cue?

options.a: Keep the side kick; sagittal means hip motion out to the side
options.b: Return the leg to a forward-back path and drop the side kick
options.c: Twist the trunk fully; rotation still counts as sagittal
options.d: Reach both arms overhead; sagittal plane applies only to the neck

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-an.explanation: Sagittal-plane knee motion is flexion and extension in a forward-back line. A side kick is frontal-plane abduction and is not the written exercise. The aide cues the path the PT described and does not add a new plane or a trunk twist.

distractorExplanations.a: Sideways kicking is frontal-plane abduction, not sagittal flexion-extension.
distractorExplanations.c: Trunk rotation is the transverse plane, not a sagittal knee bend.
distractorExplanations.d: Planes describe the path of a named joint; they are not neck-only rules.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-an.prompt: A rotator-cuff repair chart lists no active arm raise past 90°. The patient asks the aide to lift the involved arm straight overhead to hang a coat. What should the aide do?

options.a: Lift all the way up; that 90° cap is a hip, not a shoulder, rule
options.b: Move the jaw side to side instead, because the cuff holds the mandible
options.c: Stay inside the written shoulder limit and get the PT; do not force overhead
options.d: Push the arm behind the back; cuff rules only limit lumbar bending

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-an.explanation: The rotator cuff stabilizes the glenohumeral joint. A written 90° raise limit is a shoulder ROM precaution the aide must not exceed. Overhead reaching or extra internal rotation is extra motion. Call the PT rather than invent a substitute stretch at the jaw or low back.

distractorExplanations.a: Ninety degrees is a common shoulder abduction/flexion cap after cuff repair, not a hip rule.
distractorExplanations.b: The cuff does not stabilize the jaw; that is the temporomandibular joint.
distractorExplanations.d: Behind-the-back motion can stress a repair; lumbar bending is a different joint.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-an.prompt: The PT wants a rolled towel under the forefoot so the toes stay toward the shin while a drop-foot patient rests. Which ankle position is that?

options.a: Dorsiflexion: toes toward the shin, not pointed at the floor
options.b: Plantarflexion: toes pointed down as in a ballet point
options.c: Knee flexion: bend the knee and ignore the ankle angle
options.d: Hip circling: spin the hip while the foot hangs pointed down

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-an.explanation: Dorsiflexion brings the dorsum of the foot toward the tibia. The towel is a rest setup to hold that PT-ordered ankle angle, not a PTA-level goniometry test. Pointing the toes is plantarflexion, the opposite rest position for many drop-foot precautions.

distractorExplanations.b: Pointing the toes is plantarflexion, which often worsens a dropped-foot rest posture.
distractorExplanations.c: Bending the knee does not set the ankle; the PT named an ankle position.
distractorExplanations.d: Hip circles change a different joint and usually leave the ankle plantarflexed.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-an.prompt: A femur-fracture note says keep the thigh supported on a pillow and do not let the long bone hang off the mat. Which bone is the femur?

options.a: The shin bone (tibia) running from the knee to the ankle
options.b: The kneecap sitting on the front of the knee joint
options.c: The upper-arm bone (humerus) from the shoulder to the elbow
options.d: The thigh bone from the hip socket down to the knee

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-an.explanation: The femur is the thigh bone between the hip and the knee. Supporting it on the pillow follows the PT’s fracture precaution so the long bone is not levered off the edge. The tibia, patella, and humerus are different bones and would leave the thigh unsupported.

distractorExplanations.a: The tibia is the shin, distal to the knee, not the thigh bone named in the note.
distractorExplanations.b: The patella is the kneecap; supporting only it still leaves the femur hanging.
distractorExplanations.c: The humerus is in the arm; a femur-fracture pillow is a lower-limb setup.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-an.prompt: The PT noted an elbow flexion contracture and wrote do not force end-range extension. The aide is positioning for rest. What does that note mean?

options.a: Shake the arm until a brief cramp pops the elbow fully open
options.b: Treat it as a fresh ligament tear and cinch a gait belt on the joint
options.c: Keep the written rest angle; do not yank a stiff, shortened joint open
options.d: Assume the muscle only lost bulk, so extra stretching is always safe

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-an.explanation: A contracture is a stiff, shortened soft-tissue limit, not a cramp you can shake out. The aide holds the rest position the PT wrote and does not add force at end range. Atrophy is loss of bulk; a sprain is an acute ligament injury—neither is a license to yank.

distractorExplanations.a: A spasm or cramp is a brief involuntary contraction, not a fixed contracture.
distractorExplanations.b: A ligament tear is a sprain; cinching a gait belt on a stiff elbow is not treatment.
distractorExplanations.d: Lost bulk is atrophy; it does not make forced end-range extension safe.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-an.prompt: The chart says NWB on the right leg. During a stand-pivot the patient plants the right foot to “test it.” What does NWB require of the aide?

options.a: Allow full load if the patient says it feels fine (that is WBAT)
options.b: Allow only the toes to kiss the floor and praise the try (TTWB)
options.c: Let about half the body weight through a walker on that foot (PWB)
options.d: Keep all weight off that limb and rest the foot as the PT ordered

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-an.explanation: NWB means no weight through that limb. Aides follow the written load, not a patient’s on-the-spot test. WBAT, TTWB, and PWB are different orders; mixing them can overload a fracture, repair, or wound the PT is protecting.

distractorExplanations.a: Weight bearing as tolerated is WBAT, which permits load the patient can accept.
distractorExplanations.b: Toe-touch weight bearing is TTWB, a separate and less strict order than NWB.
distractorExplanations.c: Partial weight bearing is PWB; NWB allows none of that load through the limb.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-an.prompt: Two weeks after ACL reconstruction the patient asks the aide to hang the heel off the plinth to force the knee straighter than the PT’s written stop. What should the aide do?

options.a: Add the extra extension; ACL precautions apply only to the neck
options.b: Stay at the written knee limit and tell the PT; do not add stretch
options.c: Stretch the thumb instead; the ACL is an IP-joint ligament
options.d: Press hard on the heel pad, because that is where the ACL was rebuilt

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-an.explanation: The ACL is a ligament inside the knee. Hyperextension hanging is extra ROM the aide must not add when the PT wrote a stop. Report the request. The ACL is not in the neck, thumb, or heel pad, so substitute stretches there do not protect the graft.

distractorExplanations.a: Cervical rules do not replace a knee ACL limit; extra extension can stress the graft.
distractorExplanations.c: Thumb IP ligaments are unrelated; stretching the thumb does not satisfy a knee precaution.
distractorExplanations.d: The heel pad is fat and skin under the calcaneus, not the intra-articular ACL.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-an.prompt: The PT’s transfer note says start supine, then log-roll to sit. The patient is lying face-down on the mat. How should the aide read that?

options.a: Face-down is prone, not supine; reposition as the PT directed
options.b: Face-down already counts as supine because the spine looks straight
options.c: Side-lying is the same as supine for this transfer sequence
options.d: Standing on the toes is an acceptable substitute for a supine start

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-an.explanation: Supine is lying on the back. Face-down is prone. Starting from the wrong surface changes the roll the PT planned and can break a spinal or shoulder precaution. Side-lying and standing are other positions, not synonyms for supine.

distractorExplanations.b: A straight-looking spine does not convert prone into supine; the contact surface is the chest.
distractorExplanations.c: Side-lying is a lateral recumbent start, a different first move than supine-to-sit.
distractorExplanations.d: Toe-standing is upright; it skips the written bed sequence entirely.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-an.prompt: A lumbar-spine precaution says log-roll as a unit. The patient starts twisting at the waist to grab a phone on the nightstand. What should the aide do?

options.a: Allow the twist; lumbar means the neck, which this order leaves free
options.b: Cue a sit-up from the tailbone so the low back can stay still
options.c: Stop the twist, keep shoulders and hips together, and hand over the phone
options.d: Pull only on the upper back; lumbar is another name for the thoracic region

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-an.explanation: Lumbar means the low back. A log-roll keeps shoulders and hips in one piece so that segment does not rotate. The aide stops the twist, completes the written roll, and brings the phone to the patient. Neck, coccyx sit-ups, and thoracic pulls are different spinal regions or motions.

distractorExplanations.a: The neck is cervical; a lumbar precaution still forbids a waist twist.
distractorExplanations.b: Sitting up from the tailbone flexes the lumbar spine, the opposite of a log-roll.
distractorExplanations.d: The upper back is thoracic; pulling it does not protect the lumbar segments.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-an.prompt: After standing-frame time the involved ankle is puffier and the sock leaves rings. The PT asked the aide to elevate as written and report the change. What did the aide most likely observe?

options.a: A fever spike that always explains a tight sock mark on the calf
options.b: A bone-bruise diagnosis the aide should enter as a new problem
options.c: A branded brace logo imprint, which rules out extra fluid
options.d: Swelling (edema) to report and elevate; do not call it a clot

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-an.explanation: Edema is swelling from extra fluid in the tissues. Aides compare sides, follow the written elevation, and tell the PT. They do not diagnose DVT, bone bruise, or infection. Fever, a brace logo, or a charted bruise label are different findings and not a substitute for reporting new puffiness.

distractorExplanations.a: Fever is a systemic sign; sock rings after standing still point to local swelling.
distractorExplanations.b: Aides do not diagnose bone bruises; that judgment belongs to the licensed clinician.
distractorExplanations.c: A logo mark is an imprint from gear; puffy rings after standing still suggest fluid.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-an.prompt: A dependent patient has waited a long time supine on a mat. Which sites should the aide check and offload first, as trained?

options.a: Sacrum, heels, and other bony prominences against the surface
options.b: Palms and fingertips used during a light hand-opening drill
options.c: Abdomen and anterior chest, which rest on top when the patient is supine
options.d: Fleshy mid-thigh and forearm bellies that spread load over muscle

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-an.explanation: Pressure injury risk is highest where bone meets the support surface—sacrum, heels, trochanters, scapulae, occiput. Aides reposition and report redness. Palms, the anterior trunk in supine, and bulky muscle are not the first-load bony sites.

distractorExplanations.b: Palms and fingertips are not under sustained body weight on a supine mat.
distractorExplanations.c: In supine the abdomen and chest face up, so they are not pressed into the mat.
distractorExplanations.d: Muscle bulk spreads pressure; bony prominences concentrate it.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-an.prompt: The PT’s stretch setup says forearm pronated, palm on the table. The patient turns the palm up. What should the aide cue?

options.a: Keep the palm up; that already is the pronated stretch position
options.b: Turn the palm down onto the table; that is forearm pronation
options.c: Shrug both shoulders to the ears instead of rotating the forearm
options.d: Hop in place; pronation here means an ankle-hopping drill, not the arm

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-an.explanation: Forearm pronation turns the palm down (or backward). The aide cues the written start position so the PT’s stretch hits the intended tissues. Palm-up is supination. Shoulder shrugging and ankle hops are other joints and do not replace forearm rotation.

distractorExplanations.a: Palm up is supination, the opposite of a pronated, palm-on-table setup.
distractorExplanations.c: A shrug is scapular elevation; it does not rotate the radius and ulna.
distractorExplanations.d: Ankle pronation is a different joint; this cue named the forearm.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-an.prompt: The PT asked for a cold pack over the patella after a quad set. Where does the aide place it?

options.a: Along a cervical vertebra at the base of the neck
options.b: On the shin bone from the knee down toward the ankle
options.c: On the kneecap at the front of the knee, as the PT wrote
options.d: Deep against the hip socket on the side of the pelvis

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-an.explanation: The patella is the kneecap on the front of the knee. Placing the pack there follows the written landmark. Cervical vertebrae, the tibia, and the acetabulum are other bones; icing them would miss the intended joint and can chill the wrong tissue.

distractorExplanations.a: Cervical vertebrae are in the neck, not the kneecap named in the order.
distractorExplanations.b: The shin is the tibia; a pack there sits distal to the patella.
distractorExplanations.d: The hip socket is the acetabulum of the pelvis, a different joint.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-an.prompt: After weeks of NWB the involved thigh looks smaller than the other. The PT already noted disuse atrophy. What should the aide do with that observation?

options.a: Tell the patient the muscle is growing because rest always builds bulk
options.b: Force a new stretch because smaller bulk always means a contracture
options.c: Diagnose a frozen joint from the size change and add extra ROM
options.d: Report the smaller bulk and run only the exercises the PT already wrote

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-an.explanation: Atrophy is loss of muscle bulk, often from disuse. The aide can notice a thinner thigh, tell the PT, and stick to the written program. Hypertrophy is growth, a contracture is shortening, and loss of motion is a ROM limit—the aide does not relabel those or add unprescribed stretch.

distractorExplanations.a: Growth of bulk is hypertrophy; rest and NWB tend to reduce, not increase, size.
distractorExplanations.b: A contracture is stiff shortening, not the same finding as a thinner muscle belly.
distractorExplanations.c: Reduced motion is a separate ROM problem; aides do not diagnose or add ROM.

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-an.prompt: The plan lists bilateral ankle pumps in bed. The patient pumps only the surgical side. What should the aide cue?

options.a: Keep pumping only the surgical side; bilateral means one limb
options.b: Pump both left and right ankles; bilateral means both sides
options.c: Pump only at the head of the bed; bilateral refers to the skull
options.d: Pump the left hand only; bilateral is a left-hand shorthand in notes

physical-therapy-aide-readiness-check-an.explanation: Bilateral means both sides. Ankle pumps written that way include the uninvolved limb, often for circulation. Unilateral would name one side. Head-of-bed and left-hand readings invent anatomy the note did not use.

distractorExplanations.a: One side is unilateral; bilateral is both, including the non-surgical ankle.
distractorExplanations.c: Bilateral is not a skull or head-of-bed term; it is left-and-right.
distractorExplanations.d: Left-hand-only is a different laterality; the plan named the ankles.
